seasons.review_body: Class of '07 landed on Prime Video in March 2023 and earned a perfect 12-critic Rotten Tomatoes score for creator Kacie Anning's confident blend of apocalyptic comedy and female ensemble drama. The premise - a tidal wave strands former classmates on their flooded school's roof during a ten-year reunion - functions as both genre conceit and sharp social observation: the social hierarchies of high school do not dissolve under existential threat, they calcify. Critics praised Emily Browning, Megan Smart, and Caitlin Stasey as the core trio, noting the show's skill at using the survival framework to excavate the emotional wreckage of female friendship and the long afterlife of teenage dynamics. Paste Magazine called it a love letter to female friendships; Decider praised its ability to lighten the tone without deflating the stakes.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Class Of 07 S1E1: "Pilot" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The flood arrives as noise, interruption, and bodies suddenly needing instructions. “Pull me back, pull me back!” repeats until the reunion’s social theatre collapses into something uglier and more useful. Before that, the hour lets people talk over **Zoe**, mock her, redirect her, label her, and file her panic under drama. The pilot’s strongest idea is simple: a woman who looks ridiculous in ordinary life may still be right when the world starts cracking.

## Rejection as a Disaster Drill

The opening rejection is a smart first move because it teaches the episode’s social grammar before the flood teaches its survival grammar. Zoe is told the speaker is not her match, and the phrasing lands with blunt finality: “but I'm not that man.” The scene then gets nastier, more public, and more humiliating, with a proposal of being a better match mocked while “15 people stood around filming.” That detail matters. The pilot opens with heartbreak as group content.

That early beat frames Zoe as someone whose private collapse has already become public material. By the time the reunion begins judging her, the hour has done the groundwork. Zoe is not entering Ridge Heights as a neutral former classmate. She arrives carrying a recent image of herself as the woman everyone can safely laugh at. The writing uses that baggage well. Her later insistence that something is wrong has to compete with the room’s existing category for her: dramatic, needy, exposed.

The flaw is that the opening’s mechanics remain a little hazy from the available beats. The “match” language, the filming, and the insult-heavy escalation point to a sharply comic public rejection, but the pilot withholds enough connective tissue that the scene risks feeling like a punchline before it becomes a wound. As a thematic launch, it lands. First Zoe is rejected by one person. Then she has to fight being rejected by an entire room.

## Ten Years, One Room, No Clean Slate

The reunion reveal is cleanly comic. “Is this our reunion?” gets the practical answer: ten years have passed, and the room will behave accordingly. That one exchange locks the pilot into a useful pressure cooker. Nobody enters as who they are today alone. Everyone arrives dragging old versions of themselves, and the event gives those old labels a microphone.

The hour’s dialogue density helps that idea. Early reunion banter comes fast, with interruptions and social corrections doing as much work as exposition. A selection timeline is discussed, even swerving into pre-selection “in 2036,” and the point is social noise more than chronological clarity. People are trying to define the event while the event is already slipping out of their control. The pilot understands reunion talk as a sport: people measure, compare, cut each other down, and pretend the scoreboard is casual.

That is why the disaster language initially gets shrunk. When the group addresses the room as “Ladies of Ridge Heights!” and treats the crisis as “just a flash flood,” the phrasing is funny because it is so inadequate. The old institution still wants ceremony. The water does not care. The pilot’s best joke is a mismatch of scale: reunion etiquette trying to manage apocalypse-adjacent panic with school assembly energy.

## Zoe Needs Belief, Sandy Needs Control

The central conflict sharpens when **Sandy** becomes the social brake on Zoe’s alarm. Zoe wants to convince the others that the earlier flooding and cracks were real. Sandy wants Zoe seen as changed, or at least less dramatic, and repeatedly frames her as exaggerating and fame-seeking. That contradiction gives the episode a workable emotional engine. The flood is external. The fight is over credibility.

Zoe’s line, “Nobody listened to me,” is the hour’s thesis in miniature. It is also more complicated than simple vindication. She insists she tried to warn them, then interprets the disaster through the wound of being ignored. That does not make her wrong. It makes her human, and more interesting than a clean Cassandra figure. The pilot allows her self-defense to tilt into self-mythology: she reframes herself as someone who saved lives, which may be emotionally true to her even as the room resists accepting it.

Sandy’s “disappointment” framing gives the conflict bite because it attacks identity rather than logistics. She is not just saying Zoe misread the situation. She is attacking the type of person Zoe is. That is a stronger pilot choice than making the argument about flood facts alone. The real battle is classification: warning or performance, survival instinct or old drama in new clothes.

## Birds, Cracks, and the Comedy of Bad Explanations

The bird-shit fear beat is the pilot’s strangest useful texture. After birds are flying around in circles during the disaster, the conversation turns to whether it is reasonable to be afraid of birds. That could look like throwaway absurdity. In the hour’s structure, it helps. Zoe is trying to translate fear into evidence, and the show keeps handing her details that sound ridiculous when spoken aloud.

That is an effective comic trap. “Cracks started opening up” and something “gushing out” are open loops with genuine danger built into them, but they also sound like the kind of phrases a room full of skeptical former classmates can mock into nonsense. The pilot gets tension from that gap. The more Zoe explains, the more explanation itself becomes a liability. Disaster in this episode includes water rising and language failing under social pressure.

Still, the hour leans on withholding. The questions it plants are strong: why the reunion proceeds despite contact and RSVP issues, what exactly happened with the cracks, whether “Laura Cunningham” being “not dead” is credible or a flood-crisis misunderstanding. A pilot has to decide how much opacity is intrigue and how much is fog. Here, the balance mostly works, though the middle stretch could use one firmer visual or factual anchor to make Zoe’s warning feel less abstract before the flood takes over.

## Panic Gives the Pilot Its Shape

The best rhythm arrives when the banter breaks into directives. “Ladies!... stay calm!” and the repeated “Pull me back!” belong to a different show language than the reunion sniping, and the shift is the point. The pilot accelerates from talk into command, from social performance into bodily risk. That acceleration gives the episode its clearest shape.

The hour is sharpest when the flood edits the room. The earlier scenes are crowded with people managing reputation. The crisis strips that down to immediate verbs: warn, pull, listen, move. Zoe’s need to be believed stops being a personality problem and becomes a survival problem. That turn is satisfying because the pilot has spent enough time making her credibility fragile.

The limitation is that some early material feels built more for noise than precision. The dialogue density creates reunion chaos, but not every exchange cuts equally. The “CliffsNotes of your life” boundary, for instance, is a neat sign of how Zoe is managed and redirected, yet the hour has so many competing fragments that a few character edges blur. The flood fixes that. Once panic arrives, the pilot knows exactly which pressure point to press.

## The Verdict

“Pilot” is a solid, spiky opener with a strong central engine: Zoe’s humiliation becomes the reason people doubt her, then the disaster makes that doubt dangerous. The episode earns its best moments by letting comedy and panic share the same room without smoothing either one down. Its social cruelty has a point, and its flood escalation gives the hour a needed physical jolt.

The score stops short of excellent because the pilot’s withholding occasionally muddies its own force. The cracks, contact issues, and reunion mechanics plant useful questions, but the episode could ground one or two of them harder before the chaos peaks. Still, as a season starter, it plants a clean arc: Zoe has to survive the flood while forcing the room to admit she saw it coming.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp opener turns Zoe’s public humiliation into a credibility test, then lets flood panic expose the room.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 4
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Episodes four and five - scripted by Romina Acurso - are the season's strongest material according to Ready Steady Cut's season review. The fourth episode is where the show's balance of raunchy comedy and genuine character warmth reaches its peak, and the competitive friendships between the women begin to feel genuinely hard-won rather than merely set up.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A shared survival task that forces two former rivals to operate as a unit for the first time.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 8
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale drew mixed reactions. Reel Mockery scored it 6/10, noting the script ran looser than earlier episodes and the humor in the final two episodes was the weakest stretch of the season. The finale's strongest material was in its relationship resolutions, and the series ended in a way that left the door open for a second season that Prime Video never commissioned.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The survivors' final confrontation on the flooded campus, where the survival question gives way to something more personal.
